title: Vasquez reports some who say God foreordained our works only in general, lest necessity or a lack of the decree follow
source_text: XX. Similem quoque sententiam quibusdam ex suis tribuit Gabriel Vasquez tomo primo in Thomam disputatione nonagesima nona capite quinto. Ubi referens varia suorum hac de re placita. Demum, inquit, aliqui hac oppressi difficultate dicunt Deum ab aeterno non voluisse opera nostra sigillatim, sed in genere tantum, & in universum definisse paratum esse cum quovis operari, juxta ipsius determinationem. Quibus subjungit illos hanc opinionem amplecti, ut defendant ex praefinitione Dei nullam necessitatem imponi nostrae voluntati contra libertatem suam. Tum etiam quia si necessarium esset Deum praefinire, & velle ab aeterno opera etiam gratiae sigillatim, sequeretur iis qui non operantur, neque vocationi consentiunt, aliquid necessarium deesse ad operandum, scilicet decretum illud, ac proinde mirum non esse si non operarentur, cum sine illo operari non possint.
pass_a_gloss: XX. A similar opinion also Gabriel Vasquez attributes to some of his own, in the first tome on Thomas, disputation ninety-nine, chapter five. Where reporting various tenets of his own on this matter. Finally, he says, some, oppressed by this difficulty, say that God from eternity did not will our works singly, but only in general, and defined in universal that he is ready to work with anyone, according to his determination. To which he subjoins that they embrace this opinion, that they may defend that from the foreordination of God no necessity is imposed on our will against its freedom. Then also because if it were necessary that God foreordain, and will from eternity even the works of grace singly, it would follow that to those who do not work, nor consent to the calling, something necessary for working is lacking, namely that decree, and therefore that it is no wonder if they did not work, since without it they could not work.
pass_b_english: Gabriel Vasquez attributes a similar view to some of his own school, in volume 1 on Thomas, disputation 99, chapter 5, where he reports their various positions on this question. 'Finally,' he says, 'some, overwhelmed by this difficulty, say that God from eternity did not will our works one by one, but only in general, and determined in a universal way that he is ready to act with anyone according to that person's determination.'

Vasquez adds that they adopt this view in order to maintain that God's foreordination imposes no necessity on our will against its freedom. A further reason is this. If God had to foreordain and will from eternity even the works of grace one by one, those who do not act and do not consent to the call would lack something necessary for acting, namely that decree. It would then be no wonder that they did not act, since without it they could not.

lemmas.gloss: did not will our works singly, but only in general
something necessary for working is lacking

choices.why: Vasquez's and his sources' verb for God's fixing acts beforehand; 'foreordain' keeps it distinct from praedefinire ('predefine') while showing the near-synonymy.
